slides.title: Purpose
bullets: Normal blood contains five kinds of leukocytes: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, basophils and eosinophils; in disease immature forms may also be found.
Differentiation of leukocytes may point to a particular disease or pathological condition and may also be used to follow the patient during treatment.
Morphological assessment of cells is subjective: the work is entrusted to the most experienced worker of the laboratory, who trains and supervises less experienced colleagues.

slides.title: Materials
bullets: A stained dry film.
A counter for the leukocyte count.
A microscope with 40× and 100× (oil immersion) objectives and a 10× eyepiece.
Immersion oil and a lens cloth (to remove the oil from the objective after work).
Remove oil from the objective with a soft cloth, not alcohol: alcohol may dissolve the glue that holds the lenses.

slides.title: Counting technique
bullets: 1. With the 40× objective make sure that the colour, morphology and distribution of the cells are good: the red cells should just touch or overlap.
2. Put a drop of immersion oil near the thin end of the film and spread it evenly (the oil acts as a cover glass); identify the cell type with the 100× objective.
3. To avoid counting a field twice, move the film in alternating vertical or horizontal strips.

slides.title: Counting technique
bullets: 4. Skip the thickest parts of the film; if the objective reaches a thick part, move it the other way.
5. Tally each leukocyte seen on the counter (it stops at 100 cells); in pathology examine at least 200 cells.
6. Record all results in detail.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: Visual differential counting has three main sources of error: uneven distribution of cells in the preparation, failure to recognise cells, and statistics (the number of cells counted).
In an ordinary film neutrophils, monocytes and eosinophils lie more at the edges and lymphocytes in the middle, so the film is moved in one direction.
A badly made, badly fixed or badly stained film is the main cause of errors in recognising cells.
Counting an abnormal cell among the “normal” ones is a serious error; films with abnormalities go to the senior specialist of the laboratory for the final decision.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious; blood work is done in rubber gloves with a single-use scarifier.
Never draw material into a pipette by mouth; use a rubber bulb.
Do not use glassware with chipped edges.
